summary: A 1970 note on message data types in the early network. It deals with how data in messages might be described or categorised so different computers can interpret it. It is an early design contribution, not a standard.

eli5.summary: Computers send different kinds of information: numbers, words and more. This note talks about labelling each kind so the receiver knows what it got.

questions: what is a message type field
how do computers interpret message formats
subtitle: Labeling message types so different computers understand data.

tldr.problem: Early network systems send different kinds of data, but receiving computers do not know what type each message contains, making interpretation difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 42 proposes reserving the first eight bits of every message as a type field, with standard types understood across the network and local types for each host.
tldr.outcome: The idea was not widely adopted; the network moved to other approaches for describing message content.

today: RFC 42 is not Internet Standard and was not widely adopted. Later network protocols used different approaches, such as putting type information in protocol headers or using content-type fields in higher-level protocols.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
When computers on the early ARPA network send messages to each other, they must agree on what each message contains. One computer might send a text file, another a binary data structure, another a graphics command. Without a clear label, the receiving computer cannot know how to interpret the bytes it gets.

E.I. Ancona of M.I.T. Lincoln Laboratory proposed a simple convention: reserve the first eight bits (one byte) of every message for a type field.
sections.eli5: Different computers send different stuff. The first byte is a label saying what is inside, so the receiver knows what to do with it.

sections.title: Standard and Local Types
sections.content:
The proposal defines two categories of message types. Standard types have the same meaning across the entire network; all hosts recognize them. Local types are specific to each host or even to each user.

A standard type 0 means the message uses the receiving host's local data format. A standard type 1 means it uses the sending host's format. Standard types 2 through 7 could represent common formats like U.S. ASCII, EBCDIC, or graphical data. Local types let each installation define additional formats without coordinating across the network.
sections.eli5: Some labels are understood everywhere, like ASCII text. Others are home-made, like the special way one computer likes to store numbers.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.content:
Two system programs called X and Y would handle the type field. When a process sends a message, program Y adds the type field in the first eight bits. When a message arrives, program X reads the type field and can transform the data if needed, such as converting character sets or number formats.

As network usage grew, X and Y could become table driven, where a table specified how to transform between formats. This would let users define transformations without changing the network software.
sections.eli5: Two helper programs sit at each door: one labels outgoing mail, the other reads labels on incoming mail and converts it if needed.

sections.title: Example Types
sections.content:
The RFC suggests possible standard types including U.S. ASCII, EBCDIC (used on IBM computers), and a special TTY mode called Mod 33. Another type could point to a translation table so systems could load custom conversion rules without hardcoding them.

Local types could represent each host's own character set, such as the Lincoln writer or DEC ASCII, or local graphics formats used by specific displays and graphics systems.
sections.eli5: There could be a type for American text, one for IBM text, one for graphics, and each site adds its own special types as needed.
